title: IoT Protocols Part 2: Communication Models, REST & WebSocket APIs, IoT System Components, IoT Levels 1–6 — Exam Revision
description: Exam revision of IoT protocols, part 2: request-response, publish-subscribe, push-pull and exclusive pair communication models; REST-based and WebSocket-based communication APIs; the components of an IoT system; and IoT levels 1 to 6 with their examples.

scenes.title: Four ways IoT devices talk
lines: When an IoT device sends data, who does it talk to, and how?
In part two, we cover the four IoT communication models:
request response, publish subscribe, push pull, and exclusive pair.
Then REST and WebSocket based communication APIs, the components of an IoT system, and IoT levels one to six.

scenes.title: Request-Response model
lines: Model one: Request Response.
The client sends requests to the server, and the server responds to the requests.
When the server receives a request, it decides how to respond.
It fetches the data, retrieves resource representations, prepares the response,
and then sends the response to the client.
Each request is independent, and the server works with its resources to answer it.

scenes.title: Publish-Subscribe model
lines: Model two: Publish Subscribe. It involves publishers, brokers and consumers.
First, clients subscribe to the broker.
A publishing client publishes data to the broker, for example temp thirty two, moisture sixty.
The broker then delivers that data to every client that subscribed.
Publishers are the source of data.
Publishers send the data to topics, which are managed by the broker.
Publishers are not aware of the consumers.
Consumers subscribe to the topics managed by the broker.
When the broker receives data for a topic from the publisher, it sends the data to all the subscribed consumers.

scenes.title: Topics in Publish-Subscribe
lines: Here it is with topics.
The publisher sends messages to topics, here topic A and topic B, inside the broker.
Subscriber one gets topic A. Subscribers two and three get topic B, or both.
The broker decouples the two sides. The publisher never needs to know who is listening.

scenes.title: Push-Pull model
lines: Model three: Push Pull.
Data producers push the data to queues, and the consumers pull the data from the queues.
Here the publisher sends messages to queues, and consumer one and consumer two pull from them.
Producers do not need to be aware of the consumers.
Queues help in decoupling the messaging between the producers and consumers.
Queues also act as a buffer, which helps when there is a mismatch between the rate producers push data and the rate consumers pull data.

scenes.title: Exclusive Pair model
lines: Model four: Exclusive Pair.
It is a bidirectional, fully duplex communication model, that uses a persistent connection between the client and server.
The client sends a request to set up the connection, and the server responds, accepting the request.
Once the connection is set up, it remains open, until the client sends a request to close the connection.
After connection setup, the client and server can both send messages to each other.
Finally, a connection close request, and a connection close response.

scenes.title: REST-based communication APIs
lines: Now the communication APIs. First, REST based communication APIs.
Representational State Transfer, REST, is a set of architectural principles by which you can design web services and web APIs.
It focuses on a system's resources, and how resource states are addressed and transferred.
REST APIs follow the request response communication model.
The REST architectural constraints apply to the components, connectors, and data elements, within a distributed hypermedia system.

scenes.title: How a REST request flows
lines: Here is the flow.
A REST aware HTTP client sends an HTTP packet.
The packet holds the HTTP command, GET, PUT, POST or DELETE, and a REST payload in JSON or XML.
The HTTP server does authorization, and runs the RESTful web service.
Behind it are the resources. Each resource has a URI, and one or more representations.
In short: HTTP client, then HTTP socket with the REST payload, then the server, then the resources database.

scenes.title: REST constraints
lines: REST has six constraints.
Client server: the client and server are separated, so each can change independently.
Stateless: each request carries all the information needed. The server keeps no client state between requests.
Cacheable: responses say whether they can be cached, to improve performance.
Layered system: the client cannot tell if it talks to the server directly, or through intermediaries like proxies.
Uniform interface: resources are identified by URIs, and handled the same way through standard methods.
Code on demand: the server can send executable code to the client. This is the only optional constraint.

scenes.title: WebSocket-based communication APIs
lines: Next, WebSocket based communication APIs.
WebSocket APIs allow bi directional, full duplex communication between clients and servers.
WebSocket APIs follow the exclusive pair communication model.
First, the initial handshake, over HTTP: a request to set up the WebSocket connection, and a response accepting the request.
Then bidirectional communication, as data frames, in both directions, over the persistent WebSocket connection.
Finally, closing the connection: a close request, and a close response.
The application client talks to the server through the WebSocket, which runs over TCP.

scenes.title: Components of an IoT system
lines: An IoT system has seven components.
Device, Resource, Controller Service, Database, Web Service, Analysis Component, and Application.

scenes.title: Device, Resource, Controller Service
lines: Device: an IoT device allows identification, remote sensing, and remote monitoring capabilities.
Resource: software components on the IoT device,
for accessing, processing and storing sensor information,
for controlling actuators connected to the device,
and for enabling network access for the device.
Controller Service: a native service that runs on the device, and interacts with the web services.
It sends data from the device to the web service, and receives commands from the application, via web services, for controlling the device.

scenes.title: Database, Web Service, Analysis, Application
lines: Database: it can be either local or in the cloud, and stores the data generated by the IoT device.
Web Service: it serves as a link between the IoT device, application, database and analysis components.
It can be implemented using HTTP and REST principles, a REST service, or using the WebSocket protocol, a WebSocket service.
Analysis Component: responsible for analyzing the IoT data, and generating results in a form that is easy for the user to understand.
Application: IoT applications provide an interface that users can use to control and monitor various aspects of the IoT system.
Applications also allow users to view the system status and the processed data.

scenes.title: An IoT system example
lines: Here is a complete IoT system.
Sensors give inputs, and actuators receive outputs, from a Raspberry Pi running Node-RED.
The Pi acts as the gateway to the network, here using IFTTT.
A local user can work with it directly.
Through the network, it connects to other IoT devices like a thermostat, remote users, services like Google and Twitter, and remote systems.

scenes.title: IoT Level 1
lines: Now the IoT levels. Level one.
A level one IoT system has a single node, or device, that performs sensing and or actuation, stores data, performs analysis, and hosts the application.
Everything is local. The device, resource, controller service, database, REST or WebSocket services, and the app.
Level one is suitable for modelling low cost, low complexity solutions, where the data involved is not big, and the analysis is not computationally intensive.

Example: a home automation system. One controller handles lighting control, a smoke detector, a mailbox sensor, the doorbell, an intrusion detector, an electric pot, air conditioner control and the sprinkler.

scenes.title: IoT Level 2
lines: Level two.
A level two IoT system has a single node, that performs sensing and or actuation, and local analysis.
Data is stored in the cloud, and the application is usually cloud based.
Level two suits solutions where the data involved is big, but the primary analysis is not computationally intensive, and can be done locally.
Example: smart irrigation, sensing temperature, moisture, pressure, plant health, and connectivity.

scenes.title: IoT Level 3
lines: Level three.
A level three IoT system has a single node. Data is stored and analyzed in the cloud, and the application is cloud based.
Level three suits solutions where the data involved is big, and the analysis requirements are computationally intensive.
Example: tracking package handling.
It uses an accelerometer, to sense movement or vibrations, and a gyroscope, which gives orientation information.
A WebSocket service is used, because sensor data can be sent in real time.

scenes.title: IoT Level 4
lines: Level four.
A level four IoT system has multiple nodes, that perform local analysis. Data is stored in the cloud, and the application is cloud based.
Level four contains local and cloud based observer nodes, which can subscribe to and receive information collected in the cloud from IoT devices.
It suits solutions where multiple nodes are required, the data involved is big, and the analysis is computationally intensive.
Example: noise monitoring, using sound sensors at many locations.

scenes.title: IoT Level 5
lines: Level five.
A level five IoT system has multiple end nodes, and one coordinator node.
The end nodes perform sensing and or actuation.
The coordinator node collects data from the end nodes, and sends it to the cloud.
Data is stored and analyzed in the cloud, and the application is cloud based.
Level five suits solutions based on wireless sensor networks, where data is big, and analysis is computationally intensive.
Example: forest fire detection, to detect fire in early stages, and take action while it is still controllable.
Sensors measure temperature, smoke, weather, slope of the earth, wind speed, speed of fire spread, and flame length.

scenes.title: IoT Level 6
lines: Level six.
A level six IoT system has multiple independent end nodes, that perform sensing and or actuation, and send data to the cloud.
Data is stored in the cloud, and the application is cloud based.
The analytics component analyzes the data, and stores the results in the cloud database.
The results are visualized with the cloud based application.
The centralized controller is aware of the status of all the end nodes, and sends control commands to the nodes.
Example: a weather monitoring system.
Sensors used: wind speed and direction, solar radiation, temperature of air, water and soil, relative humidity, precipitation, snow depth, barometric pressure, and soil moisture.

scenes.title: IoT levels compared
lines: Compare all six levels in one table.
Levels one, two and three have a single node. Level one does everything locally. Level two analyzes locally but stores in the cloud. Level three stores and analyzes in the cloud.
Level four has multiple nodes with local analysis, plus observer nodes.
Level five adds a coordinator node that collects from end nodes.
Level six has independent end nodes, a cloud analytics component, and a centralized controller.

scenes.title: Exam recap
lines: Quick recap.
Request response: client asks, server answers. Publish subscribe: publishers, broker, topics, subscribers.
Push pull: producers push to queues, consumers pull. Queues decouple and buffer.
Exclusive pair: bidirectional, full duplex, persistent connection.
REST follows request response, with six constraints. WebSocket follows exclusive pair.
Seven components: device, resource, controller service, database, web service, analysis, application.
Reference: Bahga and Madisetti, Internet of Things, A Hands-on Approach, University Press, 2015.
Good luck in your exam!
